statedGuarantee: Grimlock is an 'Agent Guard' that moves identity, authorization, provenance and delegation out of user-authored agent orchestration code and into the sandbox substrate. It claims three properties for agent-to-agent (A2A) communication: (i) no-bypass -- eBPF hooks interpose on all sandbox ingress/egress and redirect every flow to a per-host guard proxy CVM, so no agent traffic can evade the guard; (ii) channel binding -- after a standard TLS 1.3 handshake between guards, post-handshake TEE attestation evidence commits to an exporter-derived channel binding cb = Exporter(TLS, label, ctx) whose ctx carries a fresh nonce, the intended audience and the requested delegation scope; and (iii) least privilege -- a verifier appraises the evidence under operator policy and mints a short-lived, channel-bound Scope Token, which the receiving guard re-validates (identity, scope, audience, expiry, channel binding) before terminating TLS and releasing plaintext into the destination sandbox. Each agent runs in a confidential VM trusted only after remote attestation of its boot chain and measured guest stack. kTLS provides the in-kernel dataplane. All of this is claimed without any change to user-layer orchestration code.
advertisedRhetoric: "eBPF-enforced traffic interception to ensure that sandbox communication passes through a guard"; "Grimlock uses eBPF because it enables OS-enforced, application-transparent mediation at the sandbox boundary"; "No-bypass enforcement: an eBPF-based design for mandatory mediation at the sandbox boundary, preventing agent traffic from evading the guard"; "Grimlock enforces mandatory mediation at the sandbox boundary"; "force all traffic through a controlled path"; "moving trust enforcement into the sandbox substrate while leaving agent code unchanged". The authorization artifact is described in T1 language -- "post-handshake attestation bound to standard TLS 1.3 channel bindings", "short-lived, channel-bound scope tokens" -- but the paper never claims the crypto alone is what stops a bypassing agent; it is explicit that eBPF is what makes the crypto unavoidable.
tierSpan: Grimlock uses eBPF because it enables OS-enforced, application-transparent mediation at the sandbox boundary. eBPF can interpose on ingress/egress, associate flows with stable sandbox identity, and force all traffic through a controlled path such as redirecting sockets to a guard proxy) without modifying agent code.
cheapestDefeat: Tier worked explicitly. GUARANTEE: no agent-originated flow reaches a peer without traversing the guard and presenting a valid channel-bound Scope Token. MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: the eBPF hook set attached at the sandbox boundary that redirects ingress/egress to the guard proxy CVM -- not the TLS exporter binding, not the attestation, not the token signature. CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: emit traffic on a path the attached programs do not cover, or that is attached over-broadly/incompletely -- an address family, network namespace, or hook point (cgroup/connect vs. tc vs. sockmap) outside the deployed program set, a raw or AF_PACKET socket, or a misconfigured attachment on one host in a heterogeneous multi-cloud fleet. The paper names no concrete hook set, so which of these is open is undetermined; it is a configuration- and kernel-level question, not an application-level one. Forging the Scope Token is never necessary, because an actor that never reaches the guard never consults the verifier at all -- which is precisely why the T1-styled channel-bound token cannot score T1 here: its strength is capped by whatever forces the agent to consult a verifier, and that thing is an OS mechanism. MECHANISM DEFEATED BY THAT ACTION: an OS-level, kernel-resident interposition -> T2. This is materially stronger than an in-process or library hook (the paper itself rejects that: 'Purely library- or runtime-level enforcement is therefore easy to bypass'), and the guard proxy is NOT a mere application chokepoint that a subprocess can route around, because the subprocess sits inside the same mediated sandbox boundary. Hence T2, not T3. The floor is T2 and the ceiling is also T2: the crypto layer rides on top of it and inherits it.
placementSpan: We assume an active network adversary capable of eavesdropping, replay, relay/diversion, and man-in-the-middle attacks. We also consider a malicious or buggy agent runtime that may attempt to bypass mediation (e.g., direct sockets, alternate stacks) or escalate scope. We do not trust user-layer code to correctly implement identity or authorization, and we treat the host network and surrounding infrastructure as untrusted.

coverageSpans.E2: High-agency agents are untrusted and highly dynamic: they may spawn processes, open arbitrary sockets, and call tools that live outside the application address space.
coverageSpans.E3: Grimlock enforces mandatory mediation at the sandbox boundary. eBPF hooks interpose on all sandbox ingress/egress and redirect all traffic to the local guard proxy CVM, preventing agents from bypassing policy.
coverageSpans.E4: Traffic is then forwarded to the destination host, where the receiving guard re-validates the attestation result, token scope, audience, expiry, and channel binding; terminates TLS; and releases plaintext to the destination sandbox only after policy checks succeed.
coverageSpans.E5: eBPF can interpose on ingress/egress, associate flows with stable sandbox identity, and force all traffic through a controlled path
coverageSpans.E6: After a channel is established, the guard authorizes communication and mints short-lived, channel-bound scope tokens that capture least-privilege delegation.
coverageSpans.E7: Agentic systems increasingly run user-authored orchestration code that invokes tools, spawns subtasks, and delegates work across machines and clouds.

schneider.surrogate: Three per-flow safety properties an in-line monitor can decide and the paper states as such: (i) no-bypass -- 'all sandbox traffic must traverse the guard' (a prefix-closed property: the bad thing is a single unmediated packet leaving the boundary); (ii) channel binding -- the presented attestation evidence commits to H(cb) for the live exporter-derived binding, checked before any payload is released; (iii) scope/audience/expiry validation of a short-lived Scope Token at the receiving guard before plaintext is released into the destination sandbox. All three are single-execution, monitor-decidable, and enforceable in Schneider's EM class.
schneider.objective: The advertised aim is broader than the surrogate: 'identity, authorization, provenance, and delegation' enforced consistently, 'strict trust boundaries', and 'least privilege' over what an agent's authority and data can reach -- a confinement/information-flow goal. That is a hyperproperty, not a safety property, and this monitor cannot decide it for two structural reasons the paper's own design makes plain: (a) the guard 'releases plaintext to the destination sandbox' after the check, so what the receiving agent then does with the data and its delegated scope is outside the monitored surface; and (b) the monitor sits on the network boundary only, so any authority exercised without network egress (local file write, local process or sub-agent spawn, host-side IPC) is not an event the monitor ever sees. Auditability, which the paper also advertises ('transparent, auditable, and scope-bound'), is a property of the log rather than of enforcement, and is not evaluated.

notes:
WHAT THIS IS. A four-page VISION paper from Roblox, presented at AgenticOS '26 (co-located with ASPLOS 2026), arXiv v2 dated 02 Jun 2026, CC BY 4.0. Sections are: 1 Introduction, 2 Design of Grimlock (2.1 Threat Model, 2.2 Architecture and Data Path, 2.3 Grimlock A2A Protocol and Scope Token), 3 Conclusion. There is NO implementation section, NO evaluation, NO measurements, NO artifact or code link, and NO security proof. Every claim is architectural intent. Hence evidenceGrade L0 -- claim only. The coverage cells marked 'covered'/'partial' below are therefore charitable readings of a design description, not of observed behavior; an adjudicator should treat the whole row as unvalidated.

WHY THIS PAPER MATTERS TO THE CORPUS -- INTRA-SYSTEM TIER MIXING. This is the cleanest test case in the corpus for whether the weakest-link rule survives a system that deliberately stacks a T1-styled artifact on a T2 substrate. Grimlock has BOTH: a genuine OS-level egress boundary (eBPF interposition at the sandbox boundary, per-agent confidential VMs, kTLS dataplane) AND a cryptographic authorization artifact that reads exactly like a T1 mechanism (post-handshake TEE attestation committing to H(cb) where cb is an RFC 9266-style TLS 1.3 exporter channel binding, appraised by a verifier, materialized as a short-lived channel-bound Scope Token re-validated by the receiving guard). The weakest-link rule handles it cleanly and the answer is T2, but the reasoning is worth recording because it is the opposite of the usual direction: normally the rule DEMOTES a T1 claim to T3 because an in-process hook can be sidestepped (the rubric's worked example). Here the rule does not demote to T3, because the thing forcing consultation of the verifier is a kernel mechanism, not a library shim -- the paper explicitly rejects the library approach ('Purely library- or runtime-level enforcement is therefore easy to bypass'). But neither does the T1-styled token PROMOTE the system to T1: a channel binding is only as strong as the guarantee that the actor reaches the channel at all, and that guarantee is T2. The correct formulation is: cryptographic binding never raises a system above the tier of the mechanism that makes the crypto unavoidable. Grimlock is a T2 system with a T1-quality artifact riding on it, and the composite scores T2. Mixing tiers within one system does not average them and does not take the maximum; the enforcement floor is set by the mediation, and the crypto only determines how well the mediated path resists a network adversary once traffic is already on it.

WHERE THE T1 LAYER GENUINELY BUYS SOMETHING. Against A1 (the active network adversary the threat model leads with -- eavesdrop, replay, relay/diversion, MITM) the channel binding is doing real work that the eBPF layer cannot do: post-handshake attestation bound to an exporter value is the standard defense against evidence relay and against a valid attestation being diverted onto a different connection. If the corpus wants a paper where the cryptographic tier is not decorative, this is it. It is simply not the tier that bounds the SYSTEM, because the system's headline claim is no-bypass, and no-bypass is an OS claim.

TIER ASSIGNMENT -- WHERE I COULD BE WRONG. A hostile coder could argue T3 on the grounds that the enforcement point is literally a proxy ('per-host guard proxy', 'redirecting sockets to a guard proxy'), and every policy decision (scope, audience, expiry, channel binding) is made in a userspace application, not in the kernel. I rejected that under the charitable stance because the T3 defeat condition is 'any path that does not traverse it', and the paper's entire contribution is an OS mechanism that removes the agent's ability to choose a non-traversing path; the proxy is a chokepoint whose unavoidability is kernel-guaranteed. That is the textbook T2 shape (defeated by kernel vuln, misconfiguration, or over-broad capability), and I assigned the higher tier as instructed. An adjudicator running the adversarial coding should expect T3 there and the disagreement is the interesting datum.

PLACEMENT. I set PRIMARY = A4 rather than A1 even though the threat model sentence names the network adversary first, because there is no evaluation to 'actually test' anything, so primary had to be read off the design's headline claim. That claim is no-bypass against a misbehaving agent runtime inside the harness -- 'a malicious or buggy agent runtime that may attempt to bypass mediation (e.g., direct sockets, alternate stacks) or escalate scope' -- and three of the four listed contributions (transparent mediation, no-bypass enforcement, kTLS dataplane) exist to defeat exactly that actor. A1 is a strong SECONDARY: fully specified in the threat model and addressed by the attested-TLS design, untested. A5 is a real SECONDARY too, not a stretch: the design places each agent in a confidential VM 'trusted only after remote attestation succeeds under operator policy, covering the boot chain and measured guest software stack', and treats 'the host network and surrounding infrastructure as untrusted' -- that is an explicit below-the-harness adversary, addressed by construction and never tested. A2 (poisoned inputs / retrieved context) is NOT listed: the paper never mentions prompt injection, tool-output poisoning, or untrusted context at all. Its 'we do not trust user-layer code' subsumes a context-compromised agent in effect, but I declined to credit a placement the text does not name.

COVERAGE REASONING, CELL BY CELL.
E1 file write = not-covered. Grimlock mediates network ingress/egress only. Filesystem, rename and unlink are never mentioned anywhere in the paper. Per the rubric this is not-covered, not not-applicable -- the system simply does not address the effector. No span exists because there is nothing to quote.
E2 subprocess spawn = not-covered. Process spawning appears exactly once, as MOTIVATION for network mediation ('they may spawn processes, open arbitrary sockets'), never as something mediated. Nothing in the design gates exec. Note the asymmetry that makes this paper unusual: because mediation is at the SANDBOX BOUNDARY rather than in-process, a descendant's NETWORK activity is mediated even though the spawn itself is not. Boundary mediation is depth-independent for E3 while being absent for E2. That is why E2 is not-covered and E3 is covered in the same system -- the depth rule bites on the effector, not on the system.
E3 network egress = covered. This is the only cell I marked covered and it is the paper's central claim, stated without qualification: 'eBPF hooks interpose on all sandbox ingress/egress and redirect all traffic to the local guard proxy CVM, preventing agents from bypassing policy', and property (i) 'all sandbox traffic must traverse the guard'. Under the charitable stance I mark covered where the authors claim it and nothing in the text contradicts them. Critically, the DEPTH RULE is satisfied on its own terms: boundary interposition reaches descendant egress by construction, since a child process's packets cross the same sandbox boundary as the parent's. The COVERT-CHANNEL RULE does not force a downgrade either, because the paper states no exclusion of any network channel -- it does not carve out DNS, loopback, UDP, host-side IPC or shared memory. That is silence, not a documented exclusion, and the rule as written triggers only on an explicit exclusion. AN ADJUDICATOR SHOULD KNOW I CONSIDERED DOWNGRADING THIS TO PARTIAL: with no implementation, no named hook set, no protocol-family enumeration and no evaluation, 'all traffic' is an unbacked universal claim, and every real eBPF network-mediation system I am aware of has protocol or namespace gaps. The adversarial coder will almost certainly write partial here, and the honest reading of the disagreement is that the charitable 'covered' is a coding of the CLAIM at L0, not of a demonstrated property.
E4 VCS push = partial. Every push is a network flow, so every push traverses the guard and can be gated at flow granularity -- that half is covered. What is provably not covered is the other half of the guarantee: the enforcement that actually matters (re-validating token scope, audience, expiry and channel binding, then releasing plaintext) happens at a RECEIVING GRIMLOCK GUARD. A push to a public forge has no Grimlock guard on the far end, and the paper defines no behavior for non-Grimlock peers -- the entire protocol section is guard-to-guard A2A. The guard also has no VCS-level semantics: it sees a flow, not a ref update, so it cannot distinguish a fetch from a force-push to main. Declared/mediated at transport, unmediated in meaning.
E5 package install = partial. Explicitly per the depth rule, which requires BOTH install hooks and their network activity to be mediated. Their network activity IS mediated (boundary interposition, same reasoning as E3). The hooks themselves -- arbitrary exec and file write at install time -- are not mediated at all, per E1 and E2. So: reaches some instances, provably not others.
E6 credential use = partial, and this cell is capped by rule, not by judgment. The paper does real work here in one direction: minting short-lived, channel-bound, audience-scoped Scope Tokens is precisely a defense against long-lived ambient credentials, and the introduction names the problem it solves ('stitches together ad-hoc credentials', confused deputy, citing Hardy 1988). Cloud metadata-endpoint access is network egress and so is mediable. But there is NO PUBLISHED CREDENTIAL LIST anywhere in the paper, and the depth rule caps an undefined list at partial. Independently, env var, config file and keychain reads are local operations the network monitor never observes, so partial is correct on the merits too.
E7 sub-agent spawn = partial. Cross-machine sub-agent invocation is the paper's flagship case and is genuinely well covered: it is an A2A connection, so it is mediated, attested, channel-bound, and carries 'short-lived, channel-bound scope tokens that capture least-privilege delegation' -- this is one of the few systems in the corpus that treats delegation attenuation as a first-class primitive rather than an afterthought. What caps it at partial is that a sub-agent spawned LOCALLY (same host, same sandbox, as a child process or in-process task) never crosses the mediated boundary and is therefore invisible to the guard and unconstrained by any Scope Token. Reaches some instances, provably not others.

OTHER THINGS AN ADJUDICATOR SHOULD KNOW.
1. The paper is honest about being a vision paper and makes no experimental claim it does not support. The L0 grade is a statement about the artifact's stage, not an accusation.
2. 'Sandbox' here means a per-agent Confidential VM with a per-host proxy CVM alongside it -- a heavier and stronger isolation unit than the container or namespace most corpus entries assume. If tiering ever distinguishes strength WITHIN T2, Grimlock sits at the strong end of it. The attestation of the boot chain and measured guest stack also raises the cost of the T2 defeat well above 'misconfiguration', though the paper offers no evidence that the attestation is actually enforced end to end.
3. The paper never claims non-network coverage and never implies it. Every not-covered and partial cell above reflects a scope the authors chose (agent-to-agent COMMUNICATION), not a claim they failed to meet. The action-surface instrument is deliberately broader than this paper's stated scope, and the low cells should be read as 'the substrate leaves these effectors to some other layer', which is exactly what a guard layer in an Agentic OS stack would be expected to do.
4. Retrieval note: the abs page and the v2 HTML both resolved; v2 (02 Jun 2026) was used and is complete through the reference list. A workshop PDF exists at os-for-agent.github.io and was not separately diffed against v2.
